analysis.one_liner: Requires all retail electricity to be renewable, all new vehicles zero-emission, and corporate farming regenerative, with transition subsidies.
analysis.headline: Introduced with zero cosponsors in the final 12 days of the congressional session, the bill died in three House committees without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required large retail electric suppliers to sell 100% renewable electricity by 2030 (80% starting 2027), vehicle manufacturers to sell only zero-emission cars and trucks on the same timetable, and publicly traded farming and livestock corporations to use regenerative practices and meet animal welfare rules. It offered grants covering up to half of compliance costs and doubled tax deductions to help covered companies pay for the transition, while denying all tax deductions to businesses that did not comply.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, utility customers and nearby communities would have gained cleaner air and reduced climate risk, since electricity, transportation, and agriculture produced over 60% of U.S. greenhouse gas emissions in 2019 according to the bill's findings. Car buyers would eventually have had only zero-emission vehicles to choose from, farmed animals would have gained enforceable welfare protections, and rural land and water would have benefited from mandated soil-conserving practices. Renewable energy equipment and electric vehicle makers would also have gained a guaranteed market.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Utility customers, car buyers, and public health

how_it_helps.text: Required retail electric suppliers selling at least 1,000 megawatt-hours a year to reach 80% renewable electricity by 2027 and 100% by 2030, with renewable defined to include wind, solar, geothermal, tidal, wave, and existing hydropower.
Required any manufacturer selling 100 or more vehicles a year to make at least 80% of new vehicle sales zero-emission by 2027 and 100% by 2030, under Clean Air Act regulations issued within 180 days.

Required publicly traded land and livestock corporations to manage at least 50% of their land and animals with regenerative practices by 2025, rising to 100% by 2030, and directed USDA to issue rules cutting their greenhouse gas emissions, including through less synthetic fertilizer and pesticide use.

Set animal welfare rules for covered facilities: no antibiotics or hormones except to treat disease, no procedures like debeaking or tail docking, access to pasture and natural behaviors for livestock, independent inspections, and public livestream video of any facility found in violation.

Created competitive grants covering up to 50% of transition costs, prioritizing suppliers, manufacturers, and corporations with the greatest financial need, and allowed covered businesses to double tax deductions for qualified climate transition costs.
Denied all business tax deductions for any company that did not comply with the act during the tax year, giving covered businesses a strong financial reason to meet the deadlines.

analysis.who_pays: Electric utilities, vehicle manufacturers, and publicly traded farming and livestock corporations would have borne the cost of rebuilding generation fleets, retooling production lines, and changing land and animal management on a roughly three-year ramp to 80%. Taxpayers would have funded the transition grants (which required a separate appropriation) and the cost of doubled deductions, and some of the industry costs would likely have been passed to consumers through electricity rates and vehicle prices.

drawbacks.text: The timetable was extremely aggressive: 80% renewable electricity and 80% zero-emission vehicle sales within roughly three years of passage, which grid operators, permitting processes, and vehicle supply chains almost certainly could not have met, raising real risks of reliability problems or price spikes for households.

A large share of the compliance bill would have landed on taxpayers: grants could cover half of companies' transition costs and qualified deductions were doubled, with no dedicated funding source specified beyond future appropriations.

The mandates were narrow in scope, applying only to suppliers selling at least 1,000 megawatt-hours, manufacturers selling 100 or more vehicles, and publicly traded farm corporations, leaving private companies and family farms outside the rules and creating an uneven playing field.

The regenerative agriculture requirement wrote a fixed list of practices into statute, giving the Agriculture Secretary little flexibility to adapt requirements to different regions, crops, or grazing systems, and the compliance-reporting burden would have fallen hardest on mid-sized producers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The goals — eliminating most emissions from the three largest emitting sectors and improving farm animal welfare — would deliver large, lasting public benefits, and the bill did pair mandates with real money (50% grants and doubled deductions) rather than pure commands. But the design had serious flaws: a three-year ramp to 80% that industry and grid operators could not realistically meet, transition subsidies flowing to large corporations with taxpayers picking up much of the bill, and narrow definitions that exempted most private farms while subjecting public companies to radically different rules, including public livestreams of violations. A more gradual, more uniformly applicable version could plausibly have achieved much of the benefit without the disruption; as written, it was more a statement of goals than an executable law.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the last two weeks of the session, never got a single cosponsor, and expired when the new Congress began, without any committee hearing or floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Adriano Espaillat introduced the bill on December 22, 2022, twelve days before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
It was referred the same day to three committees — Agriculture, Ways and Means, and Energy and Commerce — and no hearing, markup, or vote was ever recorded in any of them.
Not a single other House member, in either party, signed on as a cosponsor.
The bill expired automatically when the 117th Congress ended, and all legislation not passed by January 3, 2023 dies and must be reintroduced from scratch.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The covered industries came out ahead: electric utilities, conventional automakers, fossil fuel suppliers, and large publicly traded farming and livestock companies never faced the mandates, transition reporting, or loss of deductions. Members of Congress also avoided having to take a position on a far-reaching energy mandate, and the public received none of the bill's promised clean-air and climate benefits.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, and the only measure of support — the sponsor list — shows one Democrat and zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.note: Suppliers selling at least 1,000 megawatt-hours a year would have had to reach 80% renewable electricity by 2027 and 100% by 2030, with annual compliance reports to three agencies. Grants covering half of transition costs and doubled deductions would have cushioned the bill, but the pace left little room for incremental rate increases.

Any manufacturer selling 100 or more vehicles a year would have had to make 80% of sales zero-emission within three years and 100% by 2030, effectively ending gasoline vehicle sales on that schedule. Parts suppliers and dealers were excluded from the mandate.

industries.industry: Publicly traded farming and livestock corporations
industries.note: Corporations filing with the SEC would have had to convert half their land and livestock to a statutorily defined list of regenerative practices by 2025 and all of it by 2030, comply with greenhouse gas reduction rules, and submit to animal welfare mandates including independent inspections and public livestreams of violations. Private companies and family farms were exempt, concentrating the burden on public agribusiness.

A full shift of retail electricity to wind, solar, geothermal, tidal, wave, and existing hydropower by 2030 would have sharply reduced demand for coal and natural gas generation, and the vehicle mandate would have cut gasoline and diesel demand over time.

industries.industry: Renewable energy equipment and electric vehicle makers
industries.note: The mandates would have guaranteed a market for wind, solar, storage, and zero-emission vehicles, backed by 50% transition grants paid to their customers. The bill also required DOE rules on sourcing, recycling, and disposal of materials, with a goal of eliminating rare earth metals, which would have added costs but pushed manufacturing toward its stated direction.
